content: 1. Caruso et al. (2017a) developed a novel measure to assess women's negative experiences and concerns related to sanitation insecurity. This tool was designed to capture the multifaceted challenges women face in accessing safe and dignified sanitation facilities, as published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2. In a separate study, Caruso et al. (2017b) explored the gendered experiences of urination, defecation, and menstruation among women in rural Odisha, India. This research provided a comprehensive understanding of sanitation insecurity and its implications for women's health and well-being, as reported in BMJ Global Health. 3. Cavill, Chambers, and Vernon (2015) examined the sustainability of Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) programs, highlighting innovations and insights for improving long-term outcomes. Their findings were published in the Frontiers of CLTS series by IDS. 4. Clasen et al. (2012) developed and tested a device to assess latrine use in low-income settings, emphasizing the importance of accurate measurement in sanitation interventions. This work was published in Environmental Science & Technology. 5. Coffey et al. (2014) investigated the revealed preference for open defecation in rural India, providing insights into cultural and behavioral factors that influence sanitation practices. Their findings were published in the Economic and Political Weekly. 6. Cole (2015) discussed the integration of sanitation marketing with participatory approaches to sustain open defecation-free (ODF) communities in Malawi. This approach was documented in UNICEF's Sanitation and Hygiene Learning Series. 7. Cronin et al. (2017) analyzed the equity implications of sanitation interventions based on recent health and nutrition evidence. Their study, published in the International Journal for Equity in Health, emphasized the need for inclusive approaches to sanitation. 8. Curtis, Danquah, and Aunger (2009) conducted a review of hygiene behavior across eleven countries, identifying key factors that drive planned, motivated, and habitual hygiene practices. Their findings were published in Health Education Research. 9. De Buck et al. (2017) conducted a mixed-method systematic review to evaluate handwashing and sanitation behavior change interventions in lowand middle-income countries. This comprehensive review was published by the International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie). 10. Devine (2009) introduced the Sanitation FOAM framework, a tool for analyzing sanitation behaviors to design effective programs. This framework was developed under the World Bank's Water and Sanitation Program. 11. Dreibelbis et al. (2015) developed a multidimensional scale to assess attitudinal determinants of sanitation uptake and use. Their work, published in Environmental Science & Technology, provided a robust tool for evaluating sanitation interventions. 12. Dreibelbis et al. (2016) demonstrated the effectiveness of nudging techniques to promote handwashing among primary school students in Bangladesh, without relying on traditional behavior change communication. This study was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 13. Dreibelbis et al. (2013) proposed the Integrated Behavioral Model for Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), a framework for designing and evaluating behavior change interventions in resource-limited settings. Their systematic review was published in BMC Public Health. 14. Fisher et al. (2011) emphasized the critical role of behavior in public health interventions, particularly in sanitation and hygiene. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 15. Garn et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the impact of sanitation interventions on latrine coverage and use. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health. 16. Greenland et al. (2016a) conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Lusaka, Zambia, to evaluate a multiple behavior change intervention for diarrhea control. Their study was published in The Lancet Global Health. 17. Greenland et al. (2016b) assessed household sanitation practices associated with the uptake of serviced home toilets in Kumasi, Ghana. Their cross-sectional survey was published in Environment and Urbanization. 18. House, Cavill, and Ferron (2017) explored equality and non-discrimination in large-scale sanitation programs, emphasizing the importance of inclusive approaches. Their findings were published in the Frontiers of CLTS series by IDS. 19. Huda et al. (2012) conducted an interim evaluation of a large-scale sanitation, hygiene, and water improvement program in rural Bangladesh, focusing on its impact on childhood diarrhea and respiratory disease. Their findings were published in The Lancet. 20. Jenkins and Curtis (2005) explored the motivations behind latrine adoption in rural Benin, identifying aspirations for achieving a good life as a key driver. Their study was published in Social Science & Medicine. 21. Jenkins, Freeman, and Routray (2014) developed the Safe San Index to measure the safety of excreta disposal behaviors in India. Their work, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, highlighted the index's reliability and utility. 22. Kar and Chambers (2008) authored a handbook on Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS), providing practical guidance for implementing and scaling up sanitation programs. 23. Kulkarni, O'Reilly, and Bhat (2017) documented the lived experiences of poor urban women in India who face inadequate sanitation access. Their study, published in Gender & Development, highlighted the gendered dimensions of sanitation challenges. 24. Marseille et al. (2014) analyzed the costs and cost-effectiveness of scaling up integrated prevention campaigns for global health across 70 countries. Their findings were published in BMJ Open. 25. Mosler (2012) proposed a systematic approach to behavior change interventions in the water and sanitation sector, offering a conceptual model and guidelines. This work was published in the International Journal of Environmental Health Research. 26. Mosler, Mosch, and Harter (2018) investigated the relationship between Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) and latrine rebuilding in Mozambique, providing quantitative evidence. Their study was published in PLOS ONE. 27. Myers and Gnilo (2017) edited a learning paper on supporting the poorest and most vulnerable populations in CLTS programs, published by the CLTS Knowledge Hub. 28. Neal et al. (2016) applied behavioral science tactics, such as nudging and habit change, to address open defecation. Their work was documented by the World Bank's Water and Sanitation Program. 29. Odagiri et al. (2017) identified enabling factors for sustaining open defecation-free communities in rural Indonesia through a cross-sectional study. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 30. O'Reilly, Dhanju, and Goel (2017) explored the challenges of open defecation and latrine use in remote and rural areas of Uttarakhand, India. Their study was published in World Development. 31. Pasteur (2017) discussed monitoring, certification, and verification processes in CLTS programs, emphasizing the importance of keeping track of progress. This work was published by IDS. 32. Ram et al. (2010) evaluated the validity of structured observation as a technique to measure handwashing behavior, using acceleration sensors embedded in soap to assess reactivity. Their study was published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 33. Robinson and Gnilo (2016b) highlighted the role of smart finance in promoting rural sanitation development, as documented in the book Sustainable Sanitation for All. 34. Rosenboom et al. (2011) examined sanitation marketing strategies in Cambodia, providing insights into demand creation and supply chain development. Their findings were published in Waterlines. 35. Sahoo et al. (2015) conducted a grounded theory study on sanitation-related psychosocial stress among women in Odisha, India, across their life course. Their findings were published in Social Science & Medicine. 36. Sigler, Mahmoudi, and Graham (2015) analyzed behavioral change techniques in CLTS programs, identifying effective strategies for promoting sanitation adoption. Their study was published in Health Promotion International. 37. Thomas et al. (2013) validated remotely accessible instrumented monitoring technologies for global development programs, emphasizing their utility in sanitation interventions. Their work was published in Sustainability. 38. Thomas (2014) summarized key findings from a sanitation supply chain study in Eastern and Southern Africa, published in UNICEF's Sanitation and Hygiene Learning Series. 39. USAID (2018) conducted a desk review of market-based rural sanitation development programs, providing insights into scaling strategies. This review was part of the WASH Partnerships and Learning for Sustainability (WASHPaLS) project. 40. Velleman, Greenland, and Gautam (2013) proposed using immunization as an entry point for hygiene promotion and diarrheal disease reduction in Nepal. Their study was published in the Journal of Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene for Development. 41. Venkataramanan et al. (2015) tested the scalability of CLTS approaches in Lao PDR, documenting their findings in a learning brief. 42. Waterkeyn and Cairncross (2005) demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of Community Health Clubs in creating demand for sanitation and hygiene in Zimbabwe. Their study was published in Social Science & Medicine.
